rationale: The 0.98 Spearman correlation between homophily_violation and spectral indicates that both—one attribute-based, one structure-only—agree on a single dominant anomaly mechanism: users who deviate significantly from their neighbors' attributes. This consensus across fundamentally different approaches confirms the signal is robust. All other views show weak (local_affinity: 0.45) or negative (attr_struct_mismatch: −0.22 to −0.24) correlations, indicating they either measure unrelated properties or contradict the consensus. For fraudulent user detection, where the natural signal is attribute deviation from peers, combining these conflicting views would dilute rather than strengthen the ranking. Using homophily_violation alone captures this mechanism directly and interpretably, with conservative scoring (p99: 0.5166) that reflects genuine divergence rather than noise.

This graph's average degree (736.5) is where local_affinity explicitly degenerates: the neighbour average approaches the global mean and the comparison loses resolution. attr_struct_mismatch inherits this problem by building on the homophily-violation component. The correlations reveal weak agreement (0.114 between local_affinity and attr_struct_mismatch) and direct contradiction (-0.242 between attr_struct_mismatch and spectral), so averaging would dilute signal. Spectral avoids the architectural degeneracy of the other views and maintains positive correlation with local_affinity (0.462) without degrading in high-degree settings. Combining views that contradict each other (negative correlation) and measure different mechanisms would produce noise rather than a stronger anomaly signal. Use spectral alone.

local_affinity is degenerate for this dataset. With avg_degree=736.5, the neighbor average approaches the global mean across nodes, destroying discriminative resolution. attr_struct_mismatch is more robust because it compares rankings (attribute-space vs. network-structure) rather than collapsing neighbors into a mean. The correlation of 0.114 indicates they rank fundamentally differently and do not reinforce each other; combining a degenerate view with a working one dilutes the signal. The cross-modal ranking disagreement is better suited to the high-degree, moderate-homophily structure of this fraudulent-user detection task.

one_class exhibits documented embedding collapse (P99=0.1671, median=0.0276, known failure case) making it nearly non-discriminative. reconstruction degenerates on this graph's properties (avg degree 736.5, homophily 0.497) as documented in its failure mode. Strong negative correlation between one_class and reconstruction (-0.474) indicates they rank nodes oppositely, so fusion would add noise rather than complementary signal. attr_struct_mismatch has superior discriminative range (P99=0.9158), robust cross-modal design independent of neighborhood aggregation failure modes, and best suited to detect fraudsters whose attribute-space behavior diverges from their structural position in a high-degree graph.

one_class suffers from embedding collapse (explicitly stated degeneracy; 95% of nodes below 0.17), and density is degenerate on sparse high-dimensional attributes (our exact scenario: 25 features, 41.5% sparse). attr_struct_mismatch alone has a discriminative distribution (P99=0.92). The near-zero correlations (0.138, 0.105, -0.09) indicate the views measure nearly orthogonal signals; combining would average a strong cross-modal view with collapsed/degenerate noise. Low homophily (0.497) validates the mechanism: fraudulent users in review platforms exploit structure-attribute misalignment, making disagreement detection the appropriate anomaly signal.

For fraudulent user detection on a review platform, the core mechanism is likely a structure-attribute mismatch: coordinated fraudsters (good structural position from co-reviewing/co-rating/text similarity) paired with anomalous behavior attributes, or isolated nodes with unusual patterns that don't match expectations. attr_struct_mismatch directly targets this mechanism by measuring disagreement between attribute-space and structural rankings. It has the best score discrimination (range 0.34–0.92) and captures a fundamentally different signal than the others. The correlations are uniformly weak (< 0.2) or negative, indicating the other views measure unrelated properties—one_class contradicts reconstruction (-0.474), suggesting they actively harm each other when combined. In this high-density graph (avg degree 736.5, density 0.123), one_class likely suffers embedding collapse, reconstruction degenerates to ranking by distance from the mean, and density (LOF on sparse 25D attributes) concentrates. Combining these contradictory, degenerate signals would dilute attr_struct_mismatch's coherent fraud signal with noise.

The homophily_violation view explicitly degenerates on high-average-degree graphs. This graph has avg_degree 736.5, making neighbor attribute averages converge toward the global mean—exactly the failure mode described. The attr_struct_mismatch inherits this degradation and adds the problem of combining two incompatible rankings. The contrastive view, though operating under sparse/redundant attributes (41.6% sparsity, 17.6% duplication), still provides independent signal (ρ ≈ 0 with the others). Critically, homophily and attr_struct are weakly negatively correlated (ρ = -0.221), suggesting they contradict each other—a red flag that combining them would dilute rather than reinforce anomaly detection. The contrastive embedding-stability measure captures a different anomaly axis (node robustness under feature perturbation) that is orthogonal to the failing neighbor-relative views.

The views exhibit weak to moderate positive correlations (0.125–0.45) and some negative correlations (down to –0.221), indicating they capture different fraud signals rather than redundant evidence. Each has distinct degeneracy conditions: local_affinity and homophily_violation degenerate at high average degree (736.5 here), while community relies on strong modularity (0.249 is moderate). The cross-modal view (attr_struct_mismatch) provides orthogonal signal despite partial dependence on homophily_violation. No single view dominates—each would expose a potential weakness if used alone. The reference frame diversity (neighbor-relative, community-relative, cross-modal) suggests complementary fraud mechanisms: graph-structural anomalies, attribute outliers, and attribute-structure mismatches. Fusion of these independent signals is more robust than relying on one potentially degenerate view.

local_affinity explicitly degenerates at high average degree (we have 736.5), making it unreliable for this graph. contrastive shows a compressed score distribution (p99=0.1111) and inherently struggles with the high feature sparsity (41.6%) present here—dropping sparse attributes changes little, so all nodes appear equally stable. The three views are nearly uncorrelated (max |r|=0.114), indicating they measure different anomaly mechanisms rather than complementing each other. attr_struct_mismatch, despite sharing some high-degree concerns through its structure component, offers cross-modal differentiation: its attribute-space ranking half is unaffected by degree, and its score distribution (p99=0.9158) is healthiest. If one view reflects the true fraud mechanism, combining it with two degenerate or noisy views would dilute the signal.

local_affinity explicitly degenerates for high average degree (this graph has 736.5, unusually high), making its scores unreliable. attr_struct_mismatch inherits this degeneracy since it uses local_affinity as a component. The three views show weak to negative correlations (0.114, -0.242, 0.462), indicating they measure incompatible anomaly mechanisms rather than the same phenomenon from different angles; averaging such signals dilutes rather than strengthens. spectral avoids the high-degree failure mode, provides a focused structural signal independent of neighborhood-averaging artifacts, and delivers conservative but interpretable scores (p99=0.523) suitable for fraud detection where precision matters.

All three views show weak correlations (0.105, 0.102, −0.012), indicating they capture distinct anomaly facets. Density measures attribute-space outliers, one_class measures global embedding atypicality, and contrastive measures embedding fragility under perturbation. For fraudulent user detection where anomalies can manifest as unusual review patterns, global embedding deviations, or inconsistent behavior, these complementary perspectives offer better coverage than any single view. The weak homophily (0.497) means fraudsters may not cluster together, so relying solely on one_class could miss scattered anomalies; relying solely on density ignores graph-structural signals. No single view dominates the others, and each has degeneration risks (one_class embedding collapse, density with sparse attributes, contrastive with redundant attributes). Combining them averages these risks and leverages orthogonal signals rather than diluting complementary information.

The three views are measuring fundamentally different mechanisms and partially contradict each other (one_class vs adversarial: -0.191, density vs adversarial: -0.099), indicating that combining them would dilute rather than amplify signal. Adversarial is the strongest choice: it has the widest discriminative range (0.613–0.8049), incorporates graph structure via GCN (critical for a 736-node-average-degree graph), and directly measures attribute authenticity—a strong proxy for fraudulent behavior. Density operates only on attributes and ignores the rich relational structure. One-class suffers from known embedding-collapse issues and exhibits a suspiciously tight score range, suggesting reduced discriminative power. For fraud detection on a social graph, relying on the adversarial view alone avoids the harmful conflation of contradictory signals.

The three views are nearly decorrelated (all Spearman correlations < 0.14), indicating they measure fundamentally different aspects with no clear complementarity. Two of them show strong degeneration indicators: contrastive suffers from the dataset's high sparsity (41.6%) and feature duplication (17.6%), producing a compressed, poorly discriminative score range (p99=0.1111); one_class exhibits documented embedding collapse, also yielding a compressed range (p99=0.1671) with minimal differentiation across nodes. attr_struct_mismatch is the only view with meaningful signal: a wide score distribution (0.34–0.92) and a principled cross-modal approach measuring disagreement between attribute-space distance and structural homophily violations. Averaging this clear signal with two degenerated views would dilute detection performance.

local_affinity explicitly degenerates on high-average-degree graphs—this graph has mean degree 736.5, triggering the documented failure mode. one_class shows signs of embedding collapse: its score p50=0.0276 and p99=0.1671 span only 0.14, indicating the Deep SVDD objective has nearly equalized all distances. The three views correlate at 0.11–0.17, too weakly to constitute complementary angles on the same signal; instead they likely represent noise from their respective degeneracies. Combining them would dilute the broader dynamic range of attr_struct_mismatch (p99=0.9158) with noise from failed detectors. attr_struct_mismatch alone, as a cross-modal disagreement measure, has the widest discriminative range and avoids both the high-degree and embedding-collapse failure modes.

The strong negative correlation (-0.474) between one_class and reconstruction indicates they rank nodes in opposite directions, suggesting fundamental disagreement about what constitutes anomaly. Combining contradictory views cancels signal rather than improving discrimination. One_class has documented degeneration risk (collapsing embeddings) and narrow score range (p50–p99: 0.0276–0.1671); reconstruction has wider discrimination (0.0042–0.3013) and captures the fraud mechanism directly: fraudsters behave differently from their neighbors. The neighborhood-smoothed reference frame aligns with how fraud manifests in user networks. Density's near-zero correlations and tight range make it least discriminative. Using reconstruction alone avoids dilution from contradictory signals and leverages its structural awareness.

The graph exhibits exceptional homophily (0.95), its strongest structural property. Homophily_violation directly targets this property—nodes deviating from their neighbors' attributes are unambiguous anomalies in such a network. While community detection is also well-supported by high modularity (0.88), the moderate correlation (0.612) between community and homophily_violation suggests they capture related phenomena, not complementary angles on the same phenomenon. Critically, attr_struct_mismatch shows weak correlation with both (0.189, 0.274) and elevated tail scores (p99=0.96 vs. 0.87–0.89), indicating it introduces noise rather than consensus. For this graph, the homophily signal is sufficiently strong that fusion would dilute rather than improve detection.

The graph exhibits exceptional properties for community-based detection: modularity of 0.88 (very high), homophily of 0.95 (very high), 35 well-defined communities, and sparse connectivity (avg degree 2.6). The community view is purpose-built for these conditions—it detects attribute deviations within natural groups, exactly where anomalies would manifest in a high-modularity network. homophily_violation is highly correlated with community (0.612), indicating redundancy. local_affinity is nearly orthogonal to all views (correlations near zero) but severely sparse (p50=0, p90=0, only p99=1), providing almost no discriminative signal despite avoiding degeneracy at low average degree. density contributes some independent information but ignores the graph's strong community structure. Combining would dilute community's targeted signal with noise from local_affinity and redundancy from homophily_violation. For this graph's properties, community alone is both most aligned with the structure and most decisive.

The graph exhibits exceptionally strong community structure (modularity 0.88, homophily 0.95), making community-relative anomalies the natural detection mechanism for this domain. The community view has a well-calibrated score distribution and aligns with the graph's strongest structural property. In contrast, local_affinity is severely degenerate (90% of nodes score 0, only top 1% carry signal), and the three views are nearly uncorrelated (max correlation 0.274), indicating they measure different things or that two are primarily noise. Combining these independent, partially noisy views would dilute the clear signal from community membership deviation rather than enhance it.

This graph exhibits exceptional modularity (0.8814) and high homophily (0.9524), indicating that natural community structure is the dominant organizing principle for anomalies. The community view has good score discrimination (p50=0.259, p90=0.601, p99=0.875) and directly captures the likely anomaly mechanism: books misaligned with their community's attribute centroid. Including local_affinity would dilute the signal—it is severely degenerate with p50=0, p90=0, p99=1.0, providing nearly no discrimination across 99% of nodes. Homophily_violation and community are highly correlated (0.612), so fusion would not add independent evidence; conversely, attr_struct_mismatch inherits degradation from its neighbor-relative half and has only weak orthogonality (0.274 correlation). Community view alone aligns with the structure that defines this network.

The graph exhibits extremely high homophily (0.95), suggesting anomalies are primarily nodes that break the strong attribute-similarity pattern. homophily_violation directly measures this. local_affinity is degenerate on this graph (p50=0.0, p90=0.0, p99=1.0, indicating it is nearly binary with minimal discrimination for ~99% of nodes), likely because high homophily makes immediate neighbors too similar to create meaningful variation. community is moderately correlated with homophily_violation (0.612) but measures the same phenomenon at a different scale. attr_struct_mismatch is uncorrelated with local_affinity (0.061), confirming the latter is not contributing independent signal. Combining all four views would dilute the primary mechanism with a degenerate view; homophily_violation alone captures the expected anomaly mechanism cleanly without introducing noise.

Very high modularity (0.88) with 35 well-separated communities indicates robust, stable community structure. The community view directly captures the natural anomaly mechanism for a book co-purchase network: nodes whose raw attributes diverge from their community centroid. With low average degree (2.6), within-community comparison is more stable than immediate neighbor averaging. homophily_violation correlates 0.612 with community—significant redundancy that would dilute the community signal. attr_struct_mismatch's near-independence (0.189-0.274) suggests it measures meta-disagreement between ranking methods rather than direct anomaly evidence. For a graph with strong modularity, the community-relative perspective is most interpretable and least prone to the neighbor-averaging degeneracy. Combining would add noise and correlation rather than complementary angles.

local_affinity is degenerate (p50=0.0, p90=0.0), making it uninformative and a liability in fusion. Between community and attr_struct_mismatch, the community view is the optimal choice for this graph. The graph has extremely high modularity (0.88) and homophily (0.95), indicating strong community structure where attributes and edges align. The community-relative view directly leverages this structure to identify within-community outliers. attr_struct_mismatch measures cross-modal disagreement, which is a weaker signal here; its low correlation with community (0.274) and extreme weakness with local_affinity (0.061) suggests it captures noise orthogonal to the primary anomaly mechanism. In a well-structured attributed graph, the direct structural view cleanly outperforms fusion with orthogonal weak signals.

The graph exhibits very high modularity (0.88) and homophily (0.95), making community structure the dominant organizing principle. The community view is not degenerate here since modularity is high, not low. The other views show weak or contradictory signals: homophily_violation correlates moderately (0.612) but measures a related phenomenon noisily; attr_struct_mismatch and density are nearly independent (−0.005), suggesting they capture opposing signals. Averaging these disparate views would dilute the clear community-based signal. The community view provides the strongest and most interpretable anomaly frame for a high-modularity graph with strong community structure.

The Amazon co-purchase graph exhibits high modularity (0.88) and high homophily (0.95), making structural community membership the dominant anomaly signal. Community-relative scoring is robust in this regime: well-defined communities (35 for 1,418 nodes) provide stable centroids for comparison. Reconstruction is essentially uncorrelated (r=-0.011) with minimal scores (p50=0.02), indicating it does not capture meaningful structure. Density (LOF on raw attributes) is weakly correlated (r=0.271) and produces low overall scores, suggesting attribute space outliers are not the mechanism. Homophily_violation is moderately correlated (r=0.612) with community but degenerates on low average degree (2.6): its neighbour averages are unstable with so few neighbours, and given extreme homophily, violations are rare noise. Combining weak or uncorrelated signals with the strong community signal dilutes rather than improves. Use community alone.

The reconstruction view exhibits severe degeneracy: p50 and p90 are identical (0.0201), indicating it fails to discriminate among ~40% of the distribution. This degeneracy aligns with its stated failure mode—with homophily at 0.95, neighborhoods are nearly uniform in attributes, so the GCN decoder reconstructs all nodes from nearly identical smoothed signals. The three remaining views are not degenerating and measure orthogonal anomaly aspects: community scoring (supported by high modularity 0.88) captures structural misfits within well-defined communities; density/LOF detects global attribute outliers independent of graph structure; homophily_violation identifies nodes breaking the graph's strong homophily pattern. Moderate pairwise correlations (0.187–0.612) confirm complementarity rather than redundancy. Combining these three provides more robust coverage of the anomaly mechanism than any single view.

The three views measure distinct aspects of anomalousness without redundancy or contradiction. Local_affinity and homophily_violation both assess neighbor-relative deviation but in different spaces (normalized cosine vs raw Euclidean), capturing scale-dependent signal differences (correlation 0.137 suggests they are measuring genuinely different aspects). Community measures community-centroid deviation independently (correlations 0.164 and 0.386 with the neighbor-based views indicate complementary rather than redundant information). The graph's strong homophily (0.887) and modularity (0.681) support both neighbor-based and community-based approaches as valid mechanisms for anomaly. No view dominates: their score distributions are comparable (p99 ranges 0.90–1.0), and the weak but consistent positive correlations indicate they are orthogonal perspectives on the same data rather than contradicting or redundant. Combining allows the fusion to identify nodes anomalous in neighbor-space (raw-scale and normalized-scale variants) and community-space simultaneously, improving robustness to different anomaly manifests.

The graph exhibits high modularity (0.681) and strong homophily (0.887), indicating that well-separated communities and aligned attribute-structure form the dominant mechanism. The community-based view directly exploits this structure, scoring nodes by deviation from their community's attribute centroid—a signal well-suited to a network where 8 distinct communities are evident and modularity is high. Combining introduces contradictory signals: attr_struct_mismatch correlates negatively with community (-0.128) and homophily_violation (-0.226), suggesting it targets structural-attribute mismatches—a rare phenomenon in a highly-homophilous graph where structure and attributes are aligned. Meanwhile, local_affinity correlates weakly with community (0.164), measuring different, local-scale deviations. Averaging these heterogeneous signals would dilute the clear community-based mechanism with contradictory or orthogonal evidence. In a graph whose primary structure is modular and attribute-aligned, the community method alone captures the dominant anomaly mechanism.

All three correlations are weak (max 0.394), indicating these views rank nodes substantially differently and capture independent aspects of anomaly. Community detects structural deviation within groups, homophily_violation detects neighbor-attribute dissimilarity, and density detects global attribute space outliers. For spam detection, multiple mechanisms are plausible: spammers may deviate from their community's norms, differ from peers, and stand out in attribute space simultaneously. Since no view dominates (no pairwise correlation exceeds 0.4), combining them integrates complementary signals from structure, locality, and attributes rather than diluting a single strong mechanism. The moderate homophily (0.63) and power-law structure support multi-faceted detection.

The four views are largely independent (Spearman correlations ranging from -0.017 to 0.394), indicating they measure fundamentally different aspects of anomalousness. Spectral is nearly orthogonal to all others (0.028, -0.017, -0.007), capturing structural high-frequency energy; homophily_violation, community, and density are weakly to moderately correlated (0.112-0.394), representing neighbor-relative, community-relative, and attribute-space perspectives respectively. For spam detection in an email network, no single view dominates—homophily_violation is most interpretable for the task (spammers differ from neighbors), but at 0.394 correlation with community and 0.112 with density, leaves substantial unmeasured variance. The diverse reference frames and independent signals (complementary rather than redundant) suggest combining will integrate multiple valid detection mechanisms without diluting any strong single signal. The sharply different score ranges (spectral and homophily reach 1.0 at p90-p99; density maxes at 0.16) reinforce that they weight evidence differently and should be fused to avoid bias toward any one anomaly signature.

For spam detection in email networks, the primary anomaly signal is behavioral deviation from peers—accounts with unusual communication patterns stand out from their neighbors. Homophily_violation directly measures this (distance between a node's attributes and its neighbors' average), and it has the most balanced score distribution (p50=0.2515, p99=1.0) compared to spectral's extreme skew (p90–p99 both 1.0) and community's excessive conservatism (p99=0.5072). Spectral is nearly uncorrelated (r=0.028) or slightly negatively correlated (r=−0.017) with the other two, suggesting it captures a different, potentially contradictory signal related to attribute magnitude rather than local deviation. While community and homophily_violation are moderately correlated (r=0.394), adding spectral would introduce uncorrelated noise and risk diluting the core spam-detection mechanism. Homophily_violation's average degree of 13 is moderate enough that the view does not degenerate as it would with much larger degrees.

Local_affinity and homophily_violation measure the same phenomenon—neighbor-relative attribute disagreement—differing only in normalization; the description states they are 'strongly related and rarely independent evidence,' and local_affinity suffers score compression (p90 and p99 both 1.0), losing discrimination. Community measures structural position within Louvain communities, which is orthogonal; its weak correlation with both attribute-based views (0.209 and 0.394) indicates they flag different nodes, suggesting the views identify conflicting anomaly patterns. For email spam detection, the primary mechanism is likely behavioral anomaly—unusual messaging attributes—rather than structural position. Homophily_violation directly captures this with better score distribution (p50=0.25, p90=0.78) than local_affinity, while avoiding dilution from the structurally-based community view, which may add noise for this domain.

The four views measure distinct aspects of anomalies with low-to-moderate agreement. Correlations peak at 0.461 (local_affinity vs homophily_violation), and most pairs show weak correlation (<0.22), indicating each view identifies different nodes as anomalous. For spam detection in Enron, spammers likely violate multiple properties: neighbor attribute agreement (local_affinity), community membership (community), and potentially attribute-space rarity (density). The graph's high homophily (0.63) and good modularity (0.50) support both neighbor-relative and community-relative methods. While local_affinity and homophily_violation are somewhat redundant (both measure neighbor-relative deviation; density contributes weakly), combining all four provides robustness across different anomaly mechanisms. A single view risks missing spammers who deviate in only one dimension.

homophily_violation and spectral are nearly uncorrelated (0.028), indicating they measure independent dimensions of anomalies: attribute deviation from neighbors vs. structural/magnitude properties. Email spam typically involves both anomalous attributes and unusual communication structure, so a single view would miss one critical signal. The moderate correlation between local_affinity and spectral (0.718) introduces some redundancy, but local_affinity contributes a normalized perspective that complements the others. Combining all three captures the multi-faceted nature of email anomalies rather than risking dilution by one incomplete view.

Homophily violation directly measures the core spam mechanism in email networks: unusual communication patterns relative to neighbors. The views show near-zero inter-correlations (most |r| < 0.03), indicating they measure fundamentally different phenomena rather than the same signal from multiple angles. Spectral is nearly orthogonal to all views and saturates at the tail, suggesting structural noise. Density ignores graph structure entirely. Community adds redundant information (moderate correlation 0.394 with homophily) without independent evidence. With strong homophily (0.63) on this graph, violations are meaningful. Combining uncorrelated signals would dilute the clear homophily-violation evidence.

local_affinity has the strongest confidence (median 0.7087, p90/p99=1.0) and validates its signal by correlating strongly with spectral (0.718). Combining with all four views would severely dilute this: the median scores are 0.7087, 0.0773, 0.2515, 0.2594, yielding a combined median ~0.30—a 58% drop. attr_struct_mismatch adds near-zero or contradictory evidence (0.046, -0.044, 0.077 correlations across all views), and homophily_violation shows minimal agreement with spectral (0.028), measuring redundancy rather than complementary aspects. local_affinity alone captures the neighbor-relative attribute deviation mechanism strongly, and spectral's agreement confirms rather than contradicts it. Averaging would dilute rather than strengthen this signal.

The four views are nearly independent (correlations ≤ 0.394), measuring structurally different anomaly mechanisms: spectral measures attribute magnitude outliers, homophily captures deviation from neighbors, attr_struct measures cross-modal disagreement, and community detects within-group deviance. Spectral's score distribution is degenerate (p50=0.0773, p90=p99=1.0), leaving half the nodes indistinguishable and unsuitable alone. The weak positive correlation (0.394) between homophily and community does not argue for dropping either; it reflects that both measure neighbor-relative deviation but via different normalization (raw vs. community-centered). The slight negative correlations suggest complementary evidence rather than contradiction: nodes anomalous by one lens may not be by another. For Enron spam, which are behavioral anomalies, multiple facets matter: unusual message attributes, isolation from expected peers, and deviation from community norms. Combining captures this multidimensional nature; any single view omits evidence.

Homophily-violation directly captures the core spam-detection mechanism: email accounts exhibiting anomalous communication patterns relative to their network neighbors. This is semantically aligned with how spam manifests in email networks—accounts that deviate from their legitimate neighbors' behavior. The spectral view has a problematic score distribution (highly concentrated at 0.0 and 1.0), suggesting poor discrimination of gradual anomalies. Attr-struct-mismatch shows weak negative correlation (−0.044) with homophily-violation, indicating partial contradiction rather than complementary evidence. Although all three views are nearly uncorrelated, combining independent but weakly-relevant signals would dilute the signal-to-noise ratio. Homophily-violation's direct measurement of neighborhood deviation is sufficient for this task.

Spectral and local_affinity show strong agreement (0.718 correlation), indicating they detect the same underlying mechanism: attribute-based distinctiveness (behavioral patterns in email activity). However, local_affinity exhibits severe saturation (p50=0.71, p90=1.0, p99=1.0), losing discrimination power across most nodes. Spectral provides superior resolution with better score gradation (p50=0.077) while capturing the same signal. The attr_struct_mismatch is essentially uncorrelated (0.046, 0.077) and measures something orthogonal: rank disagreement between attribute and neighborhood-relative perspectives, rather than actual anomalousness. For Enron spam detection, the primary mechanism is likely unusual email patterns (behavioral anomalies), not abstract rank disagreement. Using spectral alone avoids diluting this dominant signal with an orthogonal, lower-confidence metric.

The four views are largely independent (most |r| < 0.1) and measure distinct aspects without contradicting each other. Spectral captures attribute magnitude via Laplacian structure; homophily and community capture neighbor-relative and community-relative attribute deviations from different normalized perspectives; attr_struct_mismatch captures cross-modal disagreement. For spam detection in Enron, anomalies could manifest across multiple dimensions: unusual email content/frequency (spectral), deviation from communication peers (homophily), deviation from organizational community (community), and inconsistency between attribute-space and neighborhood-space views (mismatch). The near-zero correlations indicate these views rank different nodes, not that any single view is sufficiently dominant. Combining them captures complementary signals without active contradiction, improving robustness over any single mechanism.

Spectral and local_affinity strongly correlate (r=0.718), capturing the same primary anomaly mechanism: nodes with unusual attributes or structural positions. Community is essentially independent (r≈0) and measures organizational structure rather than spam-relevant deviations. For email spam detection, the dominant signal is individual-level deviation—nodes that stand out from normal communication patterns. Including community would average this sharp signal with an uncorrelated dimension, diluting detection. Spectral's score distribution (p50=0.0773, p99=1.0) also offers better anomaly separation than local_affinity (p50=0.7087), making it the single view most suitable for ranking suspected spammers.

local_affinity directly captures the spam detection mechanism: spammers deviate from their peer communication patterns. It has the strongest signal (p50=0.71, p90=1.0), indicating clear separation. While local_affinity and spectral agree strongly (0.718), combining them with community would dilute this signal: community is nearly uncorrelated with spectral (−0.017) and weakly correlated with local_affinity (0.209), with much lower scores (p99=0.507 vs local_affinity p50=0.71). For this domain, a single direct measure of peer deviation outperforms multi-view fusion that includes an orthogonal, low-signal detector.

The four views show very low inter-correlations (most ≤0.394, several near zero), indicating they capture fundamentally different aspects of anomalousness: homophily_violation measures neighbor-relative attribute matching, community measures community-relative outliers, spectral captures structural properties, and attr_struct_mismatch measures cross-modal disagreement. None of the degeneracy conditions are strongly triggered: average degree is moderate (13.08, not high), modularity is good (0.499, not low), and the graph has meaningful structure (clustering=0.32, homophily=0.63). The low correlations suggest these views identify different anomaly mechanisms rather than redundant evidence—in spam detection, multiple signals (behavioral deviation from peers, community outlier status, structural anomaly, attribute-structure mismatch) could all identify distinct spammer types. Combining complementary independent views typically outperforms any single view when no strong consensus exists. The weak negative correlations (only −0.068 to −0.044) do not indicate true contradiction, only orthogonality.

All four views are weakly correlated (max 0.394), indicating they measure fundamentally different anomaly mechanisms. Reconstruction is neighborhood-smoothed and structure-aware; homophily_violation captures direct neighbor deviations on raw attributes; community measures within-community outliers; density is pure attribute-space without graph information. The Enron network's strong modularity (0.499) and high homophily (0.63) make both local patterns and community structure relevant. The extremely weak correlations between some pairs (reconstruction–density 0.098, homophily_violation–density 0.112) show they capture orthogonal evidence. Fusing these independent signals will detect spam senders that deviate on different dimensions: those with unusual attribute profiles (density), those who stand out within their contacts (homophily_violation), those who differ from their community (community), and those whose learned structural patterns are anomalous (reconstruction). No single view has sufficient coverage.

The contrastive view is degenerate on this dataset: it has sparse (32%) and highly redundant (56.7%) features, causing the score range to collapse (p99 only 0.0132). Under feature dropout, sparse and redundant attributes change little, making all nodes appear stable regardless of anomaly status. Community and reconstruction are both viable and complementary: they correlate only moderately (0.366), measuring different anomaly signatures—community detects attribute deviation within local structure, reconstruction detects nodes poorly predicted by their neighborhoods. Spam in email networks likely manifests as both attribute outliers and structural/connectivity anomalies. Neither alone is sufficient; fusion will capture both signals without relying on the degenerate contrastive view.

local_affinity and homophily_violation are nearly identical (r=0.931), measuring the same phenomenon—graph-neighbor attribute mismatch. Combining them adds redundancy without new signal. density operates in attribute space (not graph structure) and is only moderately correlated (r≈0.41 and r≈0.37 with the others), indicating it measures fundamentally different outliers. Given this graph's high homophily (0.763) and strong modularity (0.628), the anomaly mechanism is likely nodes that violate their local community's attribute patterns—precisely what local_affinity captures. density would dilute this focused graph-based signal without sufficient independent evidence. local_affinity is chosen over homophily_violation because normalized cosine similarity is more robust to attribute scale.
